title: Ties and duplicates
idea: MEET (thinking). Repeated values and ties are edge cases: 'the highest' when two are equal, or counting when items repeat.

exercises.prompt: You find the highest of [9, 4, 9, 2]. Two items are 9. What is the highest?
options: 9 — a tie at the top still has a clear highest value
An error because of the tie
exercises.explanation: The highest value is 9, even though it appears twice. A tie doesn't break 'the biggest value' — it's still 9.

exercises.prompt: With track-the-max using 'if item > best', what happens when item EQUALS best?
options: best stays the same — equal is not greater, so no change (still correct)
exercises.explanation: Equal is not greater, so > leaves best unchanged. The final max is still correct — ties are handled fine by >.

exercises.prompt: Counting how many scores are 90 in [90, 85, 90, 90] should give 3 — duplicates each count.
exercises.explanation: Yes. Each 90 is a separate item, so all three count. Duplicates are normal data, counted individually.

exercises.prompt: Why are duplicates worth thinking about when you plan a count?
options: You must decide whether repeats each count, or count only distinct values
exercises.explanation: 'How many 90s' counts repeats; 'how many different scores' would not. Duplicates force you to clarify what you're counting.

exercises.prompt: For 'find the highest', which inputs are worth checking? (Select all that apply.)
options: A list where the biggest value repeats
A list where the biggest is at the very end
A list where the biggest is first
A list of all identical values
exercises.explanation: All four are good checks: a repeated max, the max at the end, the max first, and all-equal. Each stresses the tracking logic differently.

exercises.prompt: Finding the highest of ALL-equal values [5, 5, 5] gives...
options: 5 — every item ties, and the highest is still 5
exercises.explanation: All equal means the max is that value, 5. The tracking never updates, but best already holds 5 — correct.

exercises.prompt: Match each list to the highest value.
exercises.explanation: Ties and duplicates don't change 'the biggest value.' The highest is just the largest number present.

exercises.prompt: A tie at the top means your max-finder has a bug.
exercises.explanation: No. A tie is normal — the highest value is still clear. Using > (not >=) handles ties correctly, keeping the first-seen max.

exercises.prompt: REVIEW: in lesson from last unit, re-checking max with [5, 2, 9, 9, 1] specifically tested...
options: A tie for the highest value (two 9s)
exercises.explanation: Two 9s is a tie at the top. Checking it confirms the tracker handles duplicates and still reports 9.

options: Ties and duplicates are normal data — decide clearly what they should do
exercises.explanation: A tie still has a clear max; duplicates each count unless you say otherwise. Think these through when you plan.
